title: Artists' Fingerprints
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 3

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 29–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

Artists' Fingerprints

Works of art often bear the fingerprints of the artist who created them. Such crucial evidence usually goes unnoticed even by connoisseurs, art experts and conservators. If present, such evidence could be valuable in clarifying questions about authorship and dating.

A A The unique character of ridges on our hands has been recognised for thousands of years. The study of ancient pottery for example reveals the utilization of fingerprint impressions in the clay as a maker's mark. In prehistoric times, we find examples of hand prints in cave painting. Only as recently as 1858 did Sir William Herschel establish its use for identification. In 1888, Sir Francis Galton undertook to refine and formulate Herschel's observations. Identification by fingerprint was first adopted in England in 1905 and received general acceptance worldwide in 1908.

B B The combination of a number of characteristics in a given finger impression is specific to a particular print. The placing of reliance on fingerprint evidence has always been on the assumption (now accepted as a fact) that no two fingers can have identical ridge characteristics. Galton's mathematical conclusions predicted the possible existence of some 64 billion different fingerprint patterns. The functionality of this technique is that the probability for the existence of two identical finger impressions from different individuals is nil and no such possibility has ever been noticed in any part of the world at any time.

C C The individuality of a fingerprint is not determined by its general shape or pattern but by the careful study of its ridge characteristics. Since at a scene of crime, usually only partial prints are found, comparison of a relatively small number of characteristics is accepted in legal practice. In a judicial proceeding, a pointbypoint comparison must be demonstrated by the fingerprint expert. This is exactly the principle that must be followed in art related fingerprint issues.

D D Hands are important to creators of visual art. They can frequently be isolated from the surface they are shaping because tools like brushes get in the way. Fingertips come into play to help model and correct stray drops of paint. By carefully nudging or pushing their fingertips into fresh, still wet brush strokes, some artists can soften their marks. The fine network of ridges was stamped, literally, by artists' fingertips onto the surface of paintings in some cases.

E E With the eventual authentication of J •M• W Turner's ‘Landscape with Rainbow’ in 1993, we can see how the authentication process works. After this painting was discovered in the early 1980s, the Biros showed it to the world's leading Turner authorities and aficionados at the Tate Gallery in London. All of the experts agreed that the painting was a ragged imitation. Later, during the restoration process, fingerprints were found on the painting. Those fingerprints were appropriately documented and reviewed by an expert from the RCMP. The fingerprints on the ‘Landscape with Rainbow’ were matched with fingerprints that had been photographed on ‘Chichester Canal’, another Turner work. When John Manners of the West Yorkshire Police conducted an independent examination of fingerprints on both paintings, he concluded that the fingerprints were identical. With this new information, the skeptics changed their minds. Additionally, it is important to note that artist Turner always worked alone without assistants. This fact decreases substantially the chance of accidental contribution. Originally purchased for just a few hundred dollars, ‘Landscape with Rainbow’ later sold for almost $200000 in a 1995 auction at Phillips in London.

F F In 1998, three envelopes containing old correspondence had been purchased in an antique shop. One of the envelopes postmarked April 21915 was found to contain a drawing folded in half. The drawing depicts a woman's head. It is executed in red chalk with an inscription written in reverse with brown ink. The design is faded and worn. Some spots suggest foxing and subsequent discoloration. The paper is yellowed and contaminated.

G G The newly discovered design bears great similarity to that of the Head of St Anne by Leonardo da Vinci, in the Windsor Collection since 1629. However, the medium is different, red chalk being used instead of black. The scale of the two images is different so offsetting (copying by contact transference) is not a satisfactory explanation for the new drawing. When the paper was first examined, several fingerprints have been noticed on the verso. One of them was found clear and containing many ridges suitable for comparison, however, no analysis was done at the time due to the lack of reference material. Many of Leonardo's works are not easily accessible and fingerprint data either does not exist or is not published.

H H Remember, the endorsement methodology is based on strict considerations and rigorous procedure. Prints that are admitted for review are those that are purely from the original creative method. The samples from reference must be from an undisputed work of art with good origin. Unauthentic contributors, like paintings touched by an assistant while still wet, must be eliminated. A match is never created unless verified by at least a qualified and proficient fingerprint examiner.

Questions 33–37

Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A-I, below.

33 The fingerprint in ancient pottery

34 The science of fingerprint identification

35 The authentication of a painting

36 Landscape with Rainbow

37 When painting, artists

A might use fingers to remove unwanted paint left by brushes.
B revealed the utilization of clay.
C was first used on Galton's mathematical assumption.
D was left to identify the person who made it.
E was restored at a high expense.
F was finally determined at an appropriate price.
G has been accepted as a reliable technique.
H was preserved at the Windsor Collection.
I could be achieved by comparing with fingerprints from other sources.
